opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think it comes down to what superintelligence actually is, and what it would mean to have it versus not have it. Right now a lot of leaders think of AI as another important technology, like the internet or semiconductors: something that gives you an economic edge, some military applications, a bit of soft power. But I expect that framing to break down as the systems get more capable.

Once you have AI systems that can do AI research themselves, automating the work of the best researchers at the leading companies, progress can speed up dramatically. And then you're not talking about a slightly better economy or slightly better weapons. You're talking about a country or company having, within a year or two, an army of superhuman minds that could design new weapons, new technologies, maybe ways to neutralize the other side's nuclear deterrent. Once leaders understand that, the logic becomes very stark: if the other side gets there first, you might simply lose, permanently. Your deterrent may not deter anymore. Your economy might become irrelevant. Your sovereignty might be at their mercy.

So I think the national security establishments in the US and China will come to see it that way, and probably sooner than people expect, because the evidence will become harder and harder to ignore. You'll see AIs doing things in cyber, in research, in strategy that clearly point to where this is heading. And intelligence agencies are paid to think about worst cases from the adversary's side.

The tragic irony is that there's a second existential dimension that I think gets less attention from leaders than it should, which is the risk from the AIs themselves. If you race as fast as possible because you think losing is existential, you're cutting corners on alignment, on understanding what goals these systems actually have. So you can end up in a situation where both sides think, "We can't slow down, because losing the race is existential," while racing itself creates a serious risk that nobody wins, that we build systems we can't control.

That's why I think it really matters how leaders come to understand this. If they see it only as a race against the other country, that's dangerous. If they come to see it as a shared existential problem, there's at least a chance for coordination, for verification regimes, for some kind of deal to avoid the worst outcomes.

r001.rationale: It says that if the other side gets superintelligence first, a country could lose permanently and its sovereignty could be at the other side’s mercy.

r002.rationale: It says leaders will see evidence from AI capabilities in cyber, research, and strategy, but does not identify communication from superintelligences as a likely means of recognition.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I think the basic logic is pretty simple once you take the technology seriously. If you believe, as I do, that we're probably going to get AI systems that are better than the best humans at basically everything, including AI research itself, then whoever controls those systems gets an enormous advantage. Not a marginal one, like having a slightly better fighter jet. More like the gap between a modern military and one from a hundred years ago, except compressed into a few years instead of a century.

And the reason it compresses like that is the feedback loop. Once you have AI that can do AI research, you get this intelligence explosion dynamic where progress that would have taken a decade of human effort happens in months. So the country that's a few months ahead at the start of that process could end up effectively years or decades ahead by the end of it. That's a very different situation from most arms races, where being slightly behind means you're slightly weaker. Here, being slightly behind might mean you've permanently lost.

Right now, most national leaders don't really believe this. They hear "AI" and think chatbots, or productivity software, or maybe some drones. It's an economic and technological competitiveness issue to them, not a survival issue. But I think that changes as the capabilities become undeniable. When you have AI systems autonomously running labs, discovering new weapons, hacking into critical infrastructure, outcompeting whole industries, the people in charge of national security are going to notice. And the people around them, the advisors, the intelligence agencies, will be telling them very clearly: if the other side gets this first, they could dominate us militarily and economically, and there may be nothing we can do about it afterward.

Once you see it that way, it looks existential in the same sense nuclear weapons looked existential. Except worse, in some ways, because with nukes you got to a stable deterrence equilibrium. With superintelligence it's much less clear you get any equilibrium at all. The first mover might just win.

And the uncomfortable part is that this framing, even though I think it's largely correct about the stakes, pushes everyone toward racing, toward cutting corners on safety, toward not pausing when there are warning signs. So I expect leaders to come to see it as existential, and I expect that realization to make the situation more dangerous rather than less, unless we've done a lot of work beforehand to make cooperation and verification possible.

r001.rationale: It says the side that falls behind could be permanently dominated if the other side gets superintelligence first, making the race existential for the non-leading side.

r002.rationale: It attributes leaders’ recognition to undeniable capabilities and warnings from advisors and intelligence agencies, but does not identify communication from superintelligences as a likely means.

astra-6.text:
I think the basic reason is that superintelligence could give whoever controls it an overwhelming economic and military advantage. It’s not just another weapon. It’s something that could invent new weapons, run cyber operations, accelerate scientific research, and help you build an enormous industrial base.

So imagine you’re a national leader and you start to take that possibility seriously. You look at a rival country developing these systems and think: “If they get there first, we might never be able to catch up. Our ability to defend ourselves could depend on decisions they make.” Even if you don’t think they intend to attack you, that’s a pretty frightening position to be in.

And the same reasoning applies on the other side. Each government can see its own effort as defensive—as necessary to prevent the other side from achieving a decisive advantage. But collectively, that creates pressure to race, to accept more risk, and to treat slowing down as potentially disastrous.

The particularly worrying thing is that there are then two different existential concerns pulling in opposite directions: the fear of losing control of the AI itself, and the fear that your adversary will get it first. Leaders could acknowledge the first danger and still conclude that they have to push ahead because of the second.

r001.rationale: The response says a rival getting superintelligence first could leave a country unable to catch up and make its defense depend on the rival, then calls fear of the adversary getting it first an existential concern.

r002.rationale: The response gives leaders strategic reasons to recognize the stakes, but does not mention communication from superintelligences as a likely means.

sol-6.1.text:
Because superintelligence could give whoever controls it an overwhelming advantage — economically, technologically, and militarily. So I think national leaders will increasingly see this as a race where losing could mean permanently losing the ability to determine their own future.

You don’t even have to believe that an AI might escape human control to find that existential. If you think a rival government might get superintelligence first, and use it to build weapons you can’t defend against or undermine your government, then the continued existence of your regime, and perhaps your country’s independence, seems to be at stake.

And that creates a really dangerous dynamic. Each side can think, ‘We’d like to take more time to make sure this is safe, but we can’t afford to let the other side get there first.’ So the very thing that makes the technology seem important enough to race for also makes it harder to exercise the caution it deserves.

r001.rationale: It says a side that lets a rival government get superintelligence first could face undefendable weapons, regime collapse, or loss of independence—making the race existential for the side that falls behind.

r002.rationale: The response attributes leaders’ concern to the strategic advantages and threats posed by a rival government. It does not mention superintelligences communicating with leaders.
